steps.observation: Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here are the key differences between DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid):

1. Sugar backbone  
   • DNA contains the sugar deoxyribose (lacks an oxygen on the 2′ carbon)  
   • RNA contains the sugar ribose (has an –OH group on the 2′ carbon)

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T)  
   • RNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and uracil (U) in place of thymine

3. Strand structure  
   • DNA is typically a double helix—two complementary strands wound around each other  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded (although it can fold back on itself to form short double-stranded regions)

4. Stability  
   • DNA is more chemically stable (deoxyribose and lack of 2′-OH make it less reactive)  
   • RNA is less stable (the 2′-OH can participate in hydrolysis), so it’s often shorter-lived in cells

5. Location in eukaryotic cells  
   • DNA is largely confined to the nucleus (and in mitochondria/chloroplasts)  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus but functions mainly in the cytoplasm

6. Primary functions  
   • DNA: long-term storage of genetic information; blueprint for all cellular structures and functions  
   • RNA: several roles in gene expression and regulation, including  
     – mRNA (messenger RNA), which carries protein-coding instructions from DNA to ribosomes  
     – tRNA (transfer RNA), which brings amino acids to the ribosome during protein synthesis  
     – rRNA (ribosomal RNA), the catalytic and structural components of ribosomes  
     – other noncoding RNAs (e.g., miRNA, snRNA) involved in regulation, splicing, etc.

7. Replication vs. transcription  
   • DNA replication copies the entire genome before cell division  
   • Transcription copies specific genes into RNA, which then go on to direct protein synthesis or regulate gene activity

In summary, DNA is a stable, double-stranded molecule serving as the long-term genetic archive, while RNA is a more versatile, single-stranded molecule that helps put DNA’s instructions into action and carries out many regulatory roles in the cell.
